evidence.claim: The Barbour County Governors’ Trail links Clio, Louisville and Clayton with Eufaula in approximately 36 miles.
evidence.quote: The total length of the Trail is approximately 36 miles.

evidence.claim: It is a journey through town centers, from Clio’s highway crossroads to downtown Clayton and the Shorter Mansion in Eufaula.
evidence.quote: The Governors’ Trail begins in Clio at the intersection of SR-10 and SR-51 and continues northeast through Louisville to downtown Clayton. The Trail then turns onto State Highway 30 and extends into Eufaula where it turns north at US Highway 431 ending at the Shorter Mansion.

evidence.claim: Alabama Byways presents the route as a combination of governors’ history, historic sites and recreation, including nearby Blue Springs State Park and Lake Eufaula.
evidence.quote: In addition to the rich heritage related to former governors, the Governors’ Trail Scenic Byway also offers many other historic, scenic, and recreational resources.

evidence.claim: A legislative act designated the trail in 2000 to recognize Barbour County residents who served as Alabama governors.
evidence.quote: The Barbour County Governors’ Trail was designated by legislative act in 2000 to recognize those from Barbour County who served as Alabama governors.

evidence.claim: The byway account identifies six governors and two others who served briefly as acting governors.
evidence.quote: Over the years, the county has produced six governors, including presidential candidate George C. Wallace.

evidence.claim: That record includes John Gill Shorter’s role in writing the Confederate constitution and George C. Wallace’s stand at the University of Alabama to uphold segregation.
evidence.quote: Governor Shorter was not only a strong secessionist and states rights advocate, but also a co-author of the confederate constitution. Governor George C. Wallace’s administration is still known by people of all ages for Governor Wallace’s stand at the entrance of the University of Alabama to uphold segregation.

evidence.claim: Begin at the junction of SR 10 and SR 51 in Clio and travel northeast through Louisville to downtown Clayton.
evidence.quote: The Governors’ Trail begins in Clio at the intersection of SR-10 and SR-51 and continues northeast through Louisville to downtown Clayton.

evidence.claim: There the trail takes Highway 30 toward Eufaula, then turns north on US 431 to finish at Shorter Mansion.
evidence.quote: The Trail then turns onto State Highway 30 and extends into Eufaula where it turns north at US Highway 431 ending at the Shorter Mansion.

evidence.claim: Louisville’s spelling changed, but its pronunciation remains Lewisville.
evidence.quote: Louisville (; formerly Lewisville and still pronounced as such)

evidence.claim: When Barbour County was formed from parts of Pike and Henry counties, Louisville became its first seat before that role passed to Clayton.
evidence.quote: When Barbour County was created from portions of Pike and Henry counties, Louisville was chosen as its first county seat, serving from 1832 until 1834, when the seat was relocated to Clayton.

evidence.claim: Lumber became part of the town’s economy in 1828 and remains important; the Central of Georgia Railroad arrived in 1888.
evidence.quote: The town's economic development was significantly influenced by the arrival of the Central of Georgia Railroad in 1888. The lumber industry, established in 1828, became a cornerstone of the local economy and continues to play an important role today.

evidence.claim: Clayton’s center was laid out on a courthouse-square plan.
evidence.quote: was laid out on a central courthouse square plan.

evidence.claim: Just south of the square, Grace Episcopal Church has white clapboard siding and a steeply pitched gable roof.
evidence.quote: The church sits just south of the courthouse square in Clayton.  It is a single-story building with a steeply pitched gable roof, with simple clapboard siding painted white.

evidence.claim: Its building was completed in 1876, on land supplied by Henry DeLamar Clayton and his wife Victoria.
evidence.quote: Construction of a church building began in 1875 on a lot owned by General Henry DeLamar Clayton and his wife Victoria. The Gothic Revival style building was completed on February 26, 1876

evidence.claim: The entry and its flanking windows have Gothic arched transoms.
evidence.quote: The three-bay façade has the double-leaf entry door topped with a gothic arched, stained glass transom window.  Flanking the door are six-over-six windows topped with similar arched transoms.

evidence.claim: The county seat also marks a turn in the drive: the Governors’ Trail leaves downtown Clayton on Highway 30 for Eufaula.
evidence.quote: The Trail then turns onto State Highway 30 and extends into Eufaula

evidence.claim: At Grace Episcopal Church, Gothic arched transoms top the entry and its flanking windows.

evidence.claim: Shorter Mansion’s present appearance came after a fire and several rounds of rebuilding.
evidence.quote: Then in 1906, architect Jack McLeod undertook significant interior and exterior renovations which resulted in the present day appearance of the former residence.

evidence.claim: Eli Sims Shorter II and Wileyna Lamar Shorter built the original house in 1884–1885; it burned in 1895.
evidence.quote: The two-story masonry structure was originally built in 1884–1885 by Eli Sims Shorter II and his wife, Wileyna Lamar Shorter but burned in 1895.

evidence.claim: T. H. Adams reconstructed it that year, and Jack McLeod’s 1906 renovations shaped the house seen today.
evidence.quote: The house, was reconstructed by late 1895 by T. H. Adams

evidence.claim: In 1965 the Eufaula Heritage Association, formed to buy and restore the house, purchased it at auction.
evidence.quote: The Kennedy family moved away from the city and the house was purchased by the Eufaula Heritage Association, initially formed in order to buy and restore the house, at auction for $33,000 in 1965.

evidence.claim: The association organized Eufaula’s first pilgrimage in 1966 and continues its historic-preservation work.
evidence.quote: The Eufaula Heritage Association organized the city's first pilgrimage in 1966 and became the primary historic preservation organization in Eufaula, a role it continues to fulfill to the present day.

evidence.claim: Jack McLeod’s 1906 renovations shaped the house seen today.
